# What problems to look for when buying used motorcycle

Acquiring a pre-owned Honda Goldwing from the mid-90s, specifically models around '95 or '96, is a significant investment that requires treating the vehicle like a complex system rather than just a collection of metal and rubber. Since this will be your first bike, the lack of prior experience means you are facing a scenario where hidden defects often go undetected during a standard visual inspection. The primary goal of your inspection should be identifying components with known failure modes that are expensive to replace or difficult to diagnose without specialized tools.

One of the most critical areas to investigate on a Goldwing of this era is the electrical system. These motorcycles are notorious for developing issues with their wiring harnesses over time. Vibrations from decades of riding can cause insulation to degrade, leading to short circuits that may not be immediately apparent but can result in a non-starting condition or erratic instrument cluster behavior. When inspecting the bike, look for signs of previous electrical fires, such as melted connectors or burnt smells near the fuse box and battery terminals. Replacing a wiring harness on a Goldwing is one of the most expensive repairs due to labor intensity and part availability; if you find evidence of chronic electrical gremlins, it often signals that the entire harness needs replacement, which can cost thousands of dollars.

Engine health is another major factor where "hidden" costs reside. While the V-twin engines in these models are generally robust, they are not immune to timing belt failure. Unlike some modern automotive designs that utilize timing chains, many Goldwings from this period rely on a rubber timing belt. This component has a finite life span and must be replaced at specific mileage intervals, typically around 45,000 miles or every four years, whichever comes first. If the seller cannot provide documentation of a recent replacement, you are inheriting a ticking time bomb. A snapped timing belt will destroy the engine internals instantly, rendering the bike a total loss. During your inspection, listen closely for ticking noises from the front cover area and check the tensioner pulley for smooth rotation without play.

Suspension components also warrant deep scrutiny due to their impact on safety and comfort. The rear shock absorbers are heavy-duty units that can fail internally or lose fluid over time. A simple way to test this is by compressing the suspension fully and releasing it; if the bike bobs excessively or takes too long to settle, the damping characteristics have likely degraded. Similarly, inspect the front forks for oil leaks around the seals. While replacing fork seals is a routine maintenance task, doing so on a neglected Goldwing often reveals that the internal bearing races are worn out as well, turning a relatively inexpensive seal kit job into a comprehensive rebuild.

Brake systems require equal attention. Look for uneven pad wear or fluid contamination, which can indicate issues with the master cylinder or caliper slide pins. On older bikes, brake lines can also become brittle and prone to cracking under heat cycles. A cracked line is an immediate safety hazard that requires replacement before riding.

Finally, consider the transmission and final drive. Goldwings often use a shaft drive system, which is durable but sensitive to seal failures. If oil leaks from the primary clutch or counter-shaft area, it suggests worn seals that can lead to bearing failure. Check the drive shaft for scoring or roughness by spinning it manually; any grit or rough spots indicate internal damage that will require disassembly and repair of the entire final drive assembly.

When evaluating the purchase, remember that the cost of acquiring a used motorcycle extends far beyond the initial price tag. The decision to proceed should be based on a thorough understanding of these potential failure points and their associated repair costs. If you are unsure about any specific mechanical aspect, consulting with a specialist who understands the nuances of mid-90s Honda engineering is highly recommended before finalizing the transaction.
